standard_text: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare their sizes, locate them approximately on a number line, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., place the square root of 2 between 1 and 2, closer to 1.4).

progression.narrative:
The standard asks students to reason about numbers they cannot write exactly -- irrational numbers like the square root of a non-perfect square, or a multiple of pi. Since a calculator is not allowed, every task rests on one move: replace the irrational number with a nearby rational approximation. That move begins with the perfect squares. To approximate the square root of 30, a student finds the two consecutive perfect squares it sits between (25 and 36), so its value is between 5 and 6, and because 30 is closer to 25, the value is closer to 5 (about 5.5). The progression opens with this estimating move -- first to the nearest whole number, then placing the value on a number line -- because a student who cannot bracket the square root of 30 between 5 and 6 can neither compare it nor plot it. The error we bait throughout is the tempting shortcut of dividing the number under the root by 2 (calling the square root of 30 '15'): halving is not rooting.

Once students can approximate one irrational number, the standard turns the skill outward. They identify which two consecutive whole numbers a root falls between, then decide which of several numbers -- some rational, some irrational -- land inside a given range. From there they compare an irrational number directly to a rational one using inequalities, number lines, or words (the square root of 30 > 5 is true; the square root of 30 > 6 is false). The capstone extends the same approximation to expressions built from an irrational number and one operation -- the square root of 2 + 3, or 3 times pi -- estimating each to compare it against a rational benchmark. The through-line we keep naming: you never need the exact value, only a rational number close enough to place it, compare it, or judge an expression.

steps.rationale: The entry approximation the whole standard rests on: replace an irrational square root with the nearest whole number by finding the perfect squares it sits between.
Turns the estimate into a position: place an irrational number at its approximate spot on a number line between two integers, leaning toward the closer end.
Names the bracket explicitly -- which two consecutive whole numbers a square root falls between -- the reasoning that powers every later comparison.
Applies the bracket to many numbers at once: decide which values, rational and irrational, fall inside a given range.
The At-proficiency target: compare an irrational number to a rational number using an approximation, stated as an inequality, a number line, or in words.
The Above-proficiency extension: approximate expressions that combine an irrational number with one operation, then compare their values.

skills.name: Recall perfect squares and their square roots

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a whole number by itself to build the perfect squares up to 15 x 15, and read a square root as its inverse.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 12 x 12? What number times itself is 49?

skills.i_do_script: Build squares out of tiles first: a 1-by-1 square uses 1 tile, a 2-by-2 uses 4, a 3-by-3 uses 9 -- each count is the side times ITSELF, which is why 3 doubled (6) is not on the list. To approximate the square root of a number without a calculator, I lean on the perfect squares -- the numbers that come from a whole number times itself. Watch: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, on up to 225 (15 x 15). I know each one both ways: 7 x 7 = 49, so the square root of 49 is 7. Knowing these cold is what lets me say the square root of 30 is a little more than 5, because 30 sits just past 25.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses a perfect square with double the number, or a square root with half the number
canonical_error.example: Says 7 squared is 14 (7 + 7) instead of 49, or that the square root of 36 is 18 instead of 6
canonical_error.why: The student reads 'squared' as 'times two' and 'square root' as 'half.' Squaring is n x n; a square root asks which whole number times itself gives the value.

skills.item_template: A whole number to square, or a perfect square to root. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What is 12 x 12?
What is the square root of 49?
What is 9 squared?
What is 15 x 15?
The square root of 64 is what?
List the perfect squares from 1 to 100.

redirect_script.stop: Squared means times itself, not times 2.
redirect_script.prompt: Picture the tile square first: a 7-by-7 square holds 49 tiles, not 14. Write the number twice with a multiplication sign: 7 squared is 7 x 7 = 49. A square root runs it backward -- what times itself gives the number?
redirect_script.praise: You used the number as a factor twice -- that's a perfect square.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; the square root of 25 is 5.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch tiny tile squares under the row 1, 4, 9, 16, 25: the 3-by-3 square holds 9 tiles, not 6 -- and a 7-by-7 square holds 49 tiles, not 14.
Write the perfect squares in a row: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
What whole number times itself gives 81? What is 11 squared?
9 x 9 = 81, so the square root of 81 is 9. And 11 x 11 = 121. Each fact works both directions.
If a student says the square root of 81 is 40.5, ask 'did you halve it, or find what times itself makes 81?'
Your turn: what is 13 x 13, and what is the square root of 100?

skills.name: Order and place rational numbers on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Locate integers, halves, and decimals on a number line marked with equal intervals.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a line from 0 to 10, where does 5.5 go? Which is farther right, 4.2 or 4.8?

skills.i_do_script: A longer name does not make a bigger number -- money shows it: $3.60 is more than $3.25 even though 325 has more digits. The number line is where that becomes visible. A number line puts numbers in order from left to right, and every point has a spot based on its value. Watch a line from 3 to 4 divided into tenths: 3.4 sits four ticks past 3, and 3.7 sits three ticks before 4, so 3.7 is farther right -- it is larger. To place a decimal like 5.5, I find the whole numbers it falls between (5 and 6) and step over to the halfway tick. Ordering numbers this way is exactly how I will later place an irrational number once I know its approximate value.

canonical_error.pattern: Places or orders decimals by digit count instead of value
canonical_error.example: Puts 3.12 to the right of 3.7 because '312 is bigger than 37'
canonical_error.why: The student compares the digit strings rather than the place values. 3.12 is between 3.1 and 3.2, left of 3.7; more digits does not mean farther right.

skills.item_template: A number-line placement or an ordering of rationals. Short response.

sample_items.stem: On a line from 5 to 6, where does 5.5 fall?
Which is farther right on a number line: 4.2 or 4.8?
Order from least to greatest: 3.7, 3.12, 3.5
Between which two whole numbers does 7.4 fall?
On a line from 2 to 3 marked in tenths, which tick is 2.6?
Is 6.3 closer to 6 or 7?

redirect_script.stop: More digits does not mean farther right.
redirect_script.prompt: Say both numbers as money first: which amount is worth more? Line up the numbers by place value: 3.12 is between 3.1 and 3.2, so it sits left of 3.7. Read the tenths first.
redirect_script.praise: You ordered by value, not by how many digits -- that's reading the number line right.

vocabulary.definition: A line where every number has a position, increasing from left to right.
The equal space between two marked ticks on a number line, such as tenths or halves.

worked_example_script.text: Before any ticks: which is more money, $3.60 or $3.25? So which of 3.6 and 3.25 should land farther right on a line from 3 to 4?
Draw a line from 3 to 4 and mark tenths.
Where does 3.6 go? Where does 3.25 go?
3.6 is six ticks past 3. 3.25 is between the 2nd and 3rd ticks -- exactly halfway from 3.2 to 3.3. 3.6 is farther right, so it is larger.
If a student puts 3.25 right of 3.6, ask 'what is the tenths digit of each?'
Your turn: place 3.9 and 3.45, and say which is larger.

skills.name: Estimate a square root to the nearest whole number
skills.i_do_script: To estimate the square root of a number to the nearest whole number, I find the two perfect squares it lands between, then decide which one it is closer to. Watch the square root of 30. The perfect squares around 30 are 25 (5 x 5) and 36 (6 x 6), so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6. Since 30 is closer to 25 than to 36, the square root of 30 is closer to 5 -- about 5.5, so to the nearest whole number it rounds to 5. I am NOT dividing 30 by 2; halving would give 15, which is way too big.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the number under the root by 2 instead of estimating the root
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 30 is about 15 (30 / 2) instead of about 5
canonical_error.why: The student treats a square root like halving because both shrink the number. A square root asks which number times itself gives the value, so the square root of 30 is near 5.5, not 15.

skills.item_template: An irrational square root (easy: sqrt of 2-8). Student gives the nearest whole number. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: What is the approximate value of the square root of 7, to the nearest whole number?
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(7) ~ 2.65, between 2 and 3, closer to 3. 2 is the lower bracket; 4 is too high.

sample_items.stem: The square root of 5 is closest to which whole number?
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(5) ~ 2.24, closer to 2. Choice 5 confuses the number with its root.

sample_items.stem: What is the approximate value of the square root of 8, to the nearest whole number?
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(8) ~ 2.83, closer to 3. Choice 4 is halving (8 / 2); 8 confuses radicand with root.

sample_items.stem: The square root of 2 is closest to which whole number?
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(2) ~ 1.41, between 1 and 2, closer to 1.

redirect_script.stop: Are you halving, or finding what times itself?
redirect_script.prompt: Name the perfect squares on each side: 25 and 36 bracket 30, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6, not 15. Then pick the closer end.
redirect_script.praise: You bracketed it between perfect squares and rounded -- that's estimating a root.

vocabulary.definition: A number whose decimal never ends or repeats, like the square root of a non-perfect square.
Find a value close enough to be useful, using nearby perfect squares.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'the square root of 40' and list nearby squares: 36 = 6 x 6, 49 = 7 x 7.
Which two whole numbers is it between? Which is it closer to?
40 is between 36 and 49, so the root is between 6 and 7. 40 is close to 36, so the square root of 40 is about 6.3 -- nearest whole number 6.
If a student says 20, ask 'did you divide 40 by 2, or find what times itself is near 40?'
Your turn: the square root of 23, to the nearest whole number.

practice_problems.stem: Between which two perfect squares does 30 fall?
practice_problems.answer: 25 and 36

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 25 is 5 and the square root of 36 is 6. So the square root of 30 is between which two whole numbers?
practice_problems.answer: 5 and 6

practice_problems.stem: What is the square root of 7 to the nearest whole number?
Estimate the square root of 40 to the nearest whole number.
Jordan estimated the square root of 30. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Jordan wrote: 'the square root of 30 = 15, because 30 / 2 = 15.'
practice_problems.answer: Halving is not rooting. 30 is between 25 (5 x 5) and 36 (6 x 6), so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6 -- about 5.5, not 15.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dividing the radicand by 2.

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 8 is closest to which whole number?
The square root of a number rounds to 6. Name a non-perfect-square value it could be.
practice_problems.answer: Any of 33 to 42 except 36, for example 38 (square root about 6.2).
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: produce a radicand from a rounded root.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why the square root of 50 is about 7 and not 25.
practice_problems.answer: 50 is just past 49 = 7 x 7, so the square root of 50 is about 7.07; 25 is half of 50, which is the halving error.

activities.title: Root to Its Nearest Whole
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the square-root cards and the whole-number cards.
2. Match each root to the whole number it rounds to (the square root of 7 <-> 3).
3. Justify each match by naming the two perfect squares it sits between.
4. Debrief: which decoy was a halving trap, and how did you rule it out?

activities.title: Halving Is Not Rooting
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jordan's claim that the square root of 30 is 15 because 30 / 2 = 15.
2. Name the perfect squares just below and just above 30.
3. Write the two whole numbers the root is between, and estimate to the nearest whole number.
4. State in one sentence why halving is the wrong move.

content.worked_problem: Estimate the square root of 30. Jordan wrote 15 because 30 / 2 = 15.
content.error_step: Jordan divided 30 by 2 instead of finding the perfect squares it sits between.
content.why: 30 is between 25 and 36, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6, about 5.5.

activities.title: Bracket It
materials: Flash cards of non-perfect-square roots (sqrt of 2 to 99)
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a card showing a square root.
2. Players race to name the two whole numbers it falls between and the closer one.
3. First correct with both brackets keeps the card.
4. Debrief: which roots were hardest to place, and why?

strategy_links.why: Chanting the perfect squares and their roots gives students the brackets they need to estimate any root instantly.
Dividing the radicand by 2 is a precise, high-frequency error a quick find-and-fix targets.
Sharing which perfect square is just below and just above builds the mental bracketing that drives estimation.

questioning_prompts: Which two perfect squares does this number fall between?
Which perfect square is it closer to?
Did you divide by 2, or find what times itself is near the number?
What whole number does the root round to?
How do you know the root is not half the number?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the number under the root by 2 instead of estimating the root.
misconception_redirects.say: Name the perfect squares on each side: 25 and 36 bracket 30, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6, not 15. Then pick the closer end.
misconception_redirects.praise: You bracketed it between perfect squares and rounded -- that's estimating a root.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student always rounds down to the lower bracket regardless of closeness.
misconception_redirects.say: Check which perfect square the number is nearer to. 40 is closer to 36 than 49, so the square root of 40 rounds to 6; but 47 is closer to 49, so it rounds to 7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared the distances and rounded to the closer whole number.

quick_checks.prompt: The square root of 7 to the nearest whole number.
quick_checks.look_for: 3. An answer of 3.5 or 4 means halving; picking 2 ignores that 2.65 is closer to 3.

quick_checks.prompt: The square root of 50 to the nearest whole number.
quick_checks.look_for: 7. An answer of 25 diagnoses dividing by 2.

sentence_starters: The square root of ___ is between ___ and ___ because ___ and ___ are the perfect squares around it.
It is closer to ___, so it rounds to ___.

worked_solution.stem: Estimate the square root of 55 to the nearest whole number.

steps.math: perfect squares around 55: 49 = 7 x 7 and 64 = 8 x 8
steps.annotation: Bracket the number between perfect squares.

steps.math: so the square root of 55 is between 7 and 8
steps.annotation: The root sits between those two roots.

steps.math: 55 - 49 = 6 and 64 - 55 = 9, so 55 is closer to 49
steps.annotation: Compare the distances to each perfect square.

steps.math: the square root of 55 is about 7.4, which rounds to 7

faded_example.stem: Estimate the square root of 20 to the nearest whole number.

steps.math: perfect squares around 20: 16 = 4 x 4 and 25 = 5 x 5
the square root of 20 is between 4 and 5

steps.annotation: Which perfect square is 20 closer to?

skills.name: Plot an irrational number at its approximate location on a number line
skills.i_do_script: To plot an irrational number on a number line, I first estimate its value, then step to that spot between two whole numbers. Watch the square root of 30. It is between 5 and 6, and closer to 5 (about 5.5), so I place my point just past the halfway mark between 5 and 6. For the square root of 2, which is about 1.4, I place the point between 1 and 2, a little less than halfway. The point's home comes from the estimate -- find the two whole numbers, then lean toward the closer one.

canonical_error.pattern: Places the point using the number under the root instead of its approximate root
canonical_error.example: Plots the square root of 30 near 30 (or at 15) instead of between 5 and 6
canonical_error.why: The student marks the radicand or half of it rather than the value of the root. The square root of 30 is about 5.5, so the point belongs between 5 and 6.

skills.item_template: An irrational number and a described number line; student states the approximate location in words. Short response.

sample_items.stem: On a number line, between which two whole numbers does the square root of 30 fall, and which is it closer to?
Describe where to plot the square root of 2 on a number line from 0 to 3.
sample_items.answer: Between 1 and 2, a little less than halfway (about 1.4), closer to 1.

sample_items.stem: Where does the square root of 13 go on a number line, and toward which whole number does it lean?
Two points are on a number line: the square root of 5 and the square root of 10. Which is farther right?
sample_items.answer: The square root of 10 (about 3.2) is farther right than the square root of 5 (about 2.2).

sample_items.stem: On a line from 7 to 8 divided into tenths, near which tick does the square root of 50 sit?
sample_items.answer: Just past 7, near the first tick (about 7.1).

redirect_script.stop: Is the point near the root, or near the number itself?
redirect_script.prompt: Estimate first: the square root of 30 is about 5.5, so the point goes between 5 and 6 -- not out at 30 or at 15. Then lean toward the closer whole number.
redirect_script.praise: You placed the point at the root's estimate, between the right two whole numbers.

vocabulary.definition: The spot on a number line matching a number's estimated value, not its exact value.
A number whose decimal never ends or repeats, like the square root of a non-perfect square.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 3 to 4 marked in tenths and write 'the square root of 14.'
Between which two whole numbers is it? Which is it closer to?
14 is between 9 and 16, so the root is between 3 and 4; 14 is closer to 16, so the square root of 14 is about 3.7 -- I place the point near the seventh tick.
If a student marks the point near 14 or near 7, ask 'what is the square root of 14 worth -- about how big?'
Your turn: describe where to plot the square root of 8 on a line from 2 to 3.

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 5 is about 2.2. Between which two whole numbers does it plot?
practice_problems.answer: 2 and 3

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 40 is about 6.3. Is its point closer to 6 or 7?
Describe where to plot the square root of 30 on a number line, including which whole number it is closer to.
practice_problems.answer: Between 5 and 6, closer to 5 (about 5.5).

practice_problems.stem: On a line from 3 to 4 in tenths, near which tick does the square root of 11 sit?
practice_problems.answer: About the third tick past 3 (about 3.3).

practice_problems.stem: Priya plotted the square root of 30. Find and fix her placement.
shown_work: Priya plotted the square root of 30 at the tick labeled 15, saying '30 / 2 = 15.'
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 30 is about 5.5, so the point belongs between 5 and 6, not at 15. Priya halved the number instead of estimating the root.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: halving to place the point.

practice_problems.stem: Order these points left to right on a number line: the square root of 20, the square root of 2, the square root of 40.
practice_problems.answer: the square root of 2 (about 1.4), the square root of 20 (about 4.5), the square root of 40 (about 6.3).

practice_problems.stem: Two irrational numbers plot between 4 and 5. Name two square roots that could be, and which is farther right.
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 17 (about 4.1) and the square root of 23 (about 4.8); the square root of 23 is farther right.
practice_problems.notes: Produce your own within an interval.

practice_problems.stem: Explain how plotting the square root of 2 and the square root of 3 shows they are different numbers even though both are between 1 and 2.
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 2 is about 1.4 (left of the midpoint) and the square root of 3 is about 1.7 (right of the midpoint), so their points sit in different spots.
practice_problems.notes: Reason about closeness within one interval.

activities.title: Peg the Root
materials: A string or tape number line labeled 0 to 10
activities.instructions:
1. Stretch the number line across a table or wall, labeled 0 to 10.
2. Draw an irrational-number card and estimate its value out loud.
3. Clip a clothespin at the point between the correct two whole numbers, leaning toward the closer one.
4. Check as a group by naming the perfect squares that bracket the number.
5. Debrief: how did estimating first decide where the peg went?

activities.title: Point at the Root, Not the Number
activities.instructions:
1. Read that Priya plotted the square root of 30 at 15.
2. Estimate the square root of 30 using the perfect squares around it.
3. Write the two whole numbers the point belongs between and which it is closer to.
4. State why marking 15 is wrong.

content.worked_problem: Plot the square root of 30. Priya marked 15.
content.error_step: Priya halved 30 instead of estimating the root's value.
content.why: The square root of 30 is about 5.5, so the point goes between 5 and 6.

activities.title: Which Interval?
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the square-root cards face up.
2. Sort each card under the interval where its point would land.
3. For each card, estimate the value to justify the interval.
4. Debrief: which numbers were close to a boundary, and how did you decide?

strategy_links.why: Placing physical markers on a number line before writing the value makes 'the root lives between two whole numbers' concrete.
Plotting at the radicand or its half is a precise placement error a find-and-fix corrects.
Discussing 'closer to which end' sharpens the estimate that fixes the point.

questioning_prompts: About how big is this root -- between which two whole numbers?
Which whole number is it closer to?
Does the point go near the root's value or near the number under the root?
Is your point left or right of the halfway mark, and why?
Which of these two points is farther right?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student places the point using the number under the root instead of its approximate root.
misconception_redirects.say: Estimate first: the square root of 30 is about 5.5, so the point goes between 5 and 6 -- not out at 30 or at 15. Then lean toward the closer whole number.
misconception_redirects.praise: You placed the point at the root's estimate, between the right two whole numbers.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student places every root exactly at the midpoint of the interval.
misconception_redirects.say: Compare the distances to each perfect square. The square root of 14 is closer to 4 than to 3, so its point sits past the middle, near 3.7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You leaned the point toward the closer whole number instead of dropping it at the middle.

quick_checks.prompt: Between which two whole numbers does the square root of 30 plot, and which is it closer to?
quick_checks.look_for: Between 5 and 6, closer to 5. A point at 15 diagnoses halving.

quick_checks.prompt: Is the square root of 3 left or right of the halfway point between 1 and 2?
quick_checks.look_for: Right (about 1.7). 'Left' means the student did not estimate closely.

sentence_starters: The square root of ___ is about ___, so it plots between ___ and ___.
It is closer to ___, so I place the point ___ of the midpoint.

worked_solution.stem: Describe where to plot the square root of 40 on a number line from 6 to 7 marked in tenths.

steps.math: 40 is between 36 = 6 x 6 and 49 = 7 x 7
so the square root of 40 is between 6 and 7
steps.annotation: The point lives in this interval.

steps.math: 40 is closer to 36, so the root is about 6.3
steps.annotation: Lean toward the closer whole number.

steps.math: place the point near the third tick past 6
steps.annotation: 6.3 is three tenths past 6, not at 20.

faded_example.stem: Describe where to plot the square root of 75 on a number line from 8 to 9 marked in tenths.

steps.math: 75 is between 64 = 8 x 8 and 81 = 9 x 9
the square root of 75 is between 8 and 9

steps.annotation: Which whole number is 75 closer to, and about what tenth is that?
State which tick to place the point near.

skills.name: Identify which two consecutive whole numbers a square root lies between
skills.i_do_script: To find the range that contains a square root, I look for the two consecutive perfect squares the number falls between; their roots are the two whole numbers. Watch the square root of 30. 25 = 5 x 5 and 36 = 6 x 6, and 25 < 30 < 36, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6. I do not divide 30 by 2 -- that would suggest a range near 15, which is wrong. The two consecutive whole numbers always come from the perfect squares that hug the number.

canonical_error.pattern: Builds the range from the number itself or half of it instead of the bracketing perfect squares
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 30 is between 29 and 30, or between 14 and 15 (halving), instead of between 5 and 6
canonical_error.why: The student anchors the range to the radicand rather than to the perfect squares around it. The square root of 30 sits between the roots of 25 and 36 -- 5 and 6.

skills.item_template: A square root of a prime or composite (medium). Student selects the containing range. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: Which range contains the value of the square root of 30?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 25 < 30 < 36, so 5-6. 14-15 is halving; 29-30 uses the number itself.

sample_items.stem: Which range contains the value of the square root of 13?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 < 13 < 16, so 3-4. 6-7 is halving; 12-13 uses the number.

sample_items.stem: Which range contains the value of the square root of 55?
Which range contains the value of the square root of 90?

redirect_script.stop: Which perfect squares hug this number?
redirect_script.prompt: Find the perfect square just below and just above: 25 and 36 hug 30, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6. Don't build the range from 30 itself or from 15.
redirect_script.praise: You used the two bracketing perfect squares to name the range.

vocabulary.definition: Two whole numbers in a row, like 5 and 6, with no whole number between them.
A whole number with no whole-number square root, like 30 or 55.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'the square root of 70' and ask for the two perfect squares nearby.
Which perfect square is just below 70? Just above?
64 = 8 x 8 and 81 = 9 x 9, and 64 < 70 < 81, so the square root of 70 is between 8 and 9.
If a student says between 34 and 35, ask 'did you halve 70, or find the perfect squares around it?'
Your turn: which range contains the square root of 46?

practice_problems.stem: Which two perfect squares does 30 fall between?
practice_problems.answer: 25 and 36

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 25 is 5 and the square root of 36 is 6. The square root of 30 is between which two whole numbers?
practice_problems.answer: 5 and 6

practice_problems.stem: Which range contains the square root of 55?
practice_problems.answer: Between 7 and 8

practice_problems.stem: Which range contains the square root of 90?
practice_problems.answer: Between 9 and 10

practice_problems.stem: Devon named the range for the square root of 30. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Devon wrote: 'the square root of 30 is between 14 and 15, because 30 / 2 = 15.'
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 30 is between 5 and 6, because 25 < 30 < 36. Devon halved 30 instead of using the perfect squares that bracket it.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dividing the radicand by 2.

practice_problems.stem: Which range contains the square root of 13?
practice_problems.answer: Between 3 and 4

practice_problems.stem: The square root of a number is between 6 and 7. Name a non-perfect-square value it could be.
practice_problems.answer: Any of 37 to 48 except a perfect square, for example 40 or 45.

practice_problems.stem: Between which two whole numbers is the square root of 150? Explain without a calculator.
practice_problems.answer: Between 12 and 13, because 144 = 12 x 12 and 169 = 13 x 13, and 144 < 150 < 169.

activities.title: Name the Range
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the square-root cards.
2. Sort each under the range of two consecutive whole numbers it falls between.
3. Justify each placement by naming the perfect squares that hug the number.
4. Debrief: how do the perfect squares set the range every time?

activities.title: Squares, Not Halves
activities.instructions:
1. Read Devon's claim that the square root of 30 is between 14 and 15.
2. Name the perfect squares just below and just above 30.
3. Write the correct range of two consecutive whole numbers.
4. State why halving the number gives the wrong range.

content.worked_problem: Which range contains the square root of 30? Devon wrote between 14 and 15.
content.error_step: Devon divided 30 by 2 instead of using the bracketing perfect squares.
content.why: 25 < 30 < 36, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6.

activities.title: Root to Its Range
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the square-root cards and the range cards.
2. Match each root to the range of two consecutive whole numbers it falls between.
3. Justify each match with the two perfect squares.
4. Debrief: which decoy range came from halving?

strategy_links.why: Sharing which perfect squares hug a number trains the bracketing this skill is built on.
Halving the radicand to name a range is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects.
Rapid recall of perfect squares makes finding the bracketing range automatic.

questioning_prompts: Which perfect square is just below the number? Just above?
What are the roots of those two perfect squares?
Did you build the range from the number itself, or from the perfect squares around it?
Are the two whole numbers in your range consecutive?
How do you know the value isn't near 15?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student builds the range from the number itself or half of it instead of the bracketing perfect squares.
misconception_redirects.say: Find the perfect square just below and just above: 25 and 36 hug 30, so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6. Don't build the range from 30 itself or from 15.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the two bracketing perfect squares to name the range.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks a range whose whole numbers are not consecutive.
misconception_redirects.say: The two whole numbers must be in a row. 49 and 64 are consecutive perfect squares, so the roots 7 and 8 are consecutive -- that's your range.
misconception_redirects.praise: You named two consecutive whole numbers straight from the bracketing squares.

quick_checks.prompt: Which range contains the square root of 30?
quick_checks.look_for: Between 5 and 6. 'Between 14 and 15' diagnoses halving; 'between 29 and 30' uses the number itself.

quick_checks.prompt: Which range contains the square root of 90?
quick_checks.look_for: Between 9 and 10 (81 < 90 < 100). Any other range means the perfect-square brackets weren't found.

sentence_starters: ___ is between the perfect squares ___ and ___.
So the square root of ___ is between ___ and ___.

worked_solution.stem: Which range contains the value of the square root of 46?

steps.math: perfect squares around 46: 36 = 6 x 6 and 49 = 7 x 7
so the square root of 46 is between the roots 6 and 7
range: between 6 and 7

faded_example.stem: Which range contains the value of the square root of 110?

steps.math: perfect squares around 110: 100 = 10 x 10 and 121 = 11 x 11

steps.annotation: What are the roots of 100 and 121?

skills.name: Select all numbers within a given range
skills.i_do_script: Sometimes I'm given a range and a list of numbers -- some rational, some irrational -- and must pick every one that lands inside. I estimate each value, then check if it is greater than the low end and less than the high end. Watch: greater than 1.5 and less than 5. The square root of 10 is about 3.2 (in), 4.5 is in, the square root of 30 is about 5.5 (out, too big), and 1 is out (too small). I keep the halving trap in mind: the square root of 30 is about 5.5, not 15.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges an irrational number against the range using the radicand or half of it instead of its estimate
canonical_error.example: For 'greater than 1.5 and less than 5,' excludes the square root of 10 by treating it as 10 (too big) though it is about 3.2 and belongs in the range
canonical_error.why: The square root of 10 must first be estimated to about 3.2 before comparing; using 10 (the radicand) or 5 (halving) puts it on the wrong side of the range.

skills.item_template: A range and 5-6 numbers mixing square roots and rationals. Student selects all in range. Multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Select all numbers that are greater than 1.5 and less than 5: the square root of 3, the square root of 10, 4.5, 6, the square root of 30.
sample_items.answer: the square root of 3, the square root of 10, 4.5
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(3) ~ 1.73, sqrt(10) ~ 3.16, and 4.5 are all in (1.5, 5); 6 and sqrt(30) ~ 5.5 are too big.

sample_items.stem: Select all numbers that are greater than 3 and less than 7: the square root of 5, the square root of 40, 6.5, the square root of 55, 2.
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(40) ~ 6.3 and 6.5 are in (3, 7); sqrt(5) ~ 2.2 and 2 are too small; sqrt(55) ~ 7.4 is too big.

sample_items.stem: Select all numbers that are greater than 2 and less than 4: the square root of 5, the square root of 13, 3.5, the square root of 20, 1.5.
sample_items.answer: the square root of 5, the square root of 13, 3.5
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(5) ~ 2.2, sqrt(13) ~ 3.6, and 3.5 are in (2, 4); sqrt(20) ~ 4.5 is too big; 1.5 is too small.

sample_items.stem: Select all numbers that are greater than 4.5 and less than 8: the square root of 30, 7, the square root of 17, the square root of 50, 9.
sample_items.answer: the square root of 30, 7, the square root of 50
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(30) ~ 5.5, 7, and sqrt(50) ~ 7.07 are in (4.5, 8); sqrt(17) ~ 4.1 is too small; 9 is too big.

redirect_script.stop: Did you estimate each root before comparing?
redirect_script.prompt: Turn every square root into a decimal first: the square root of 10 is about 3.2, so it is greater than 1.5 and less than 5 -- it belongs in the range. Don't compare using 10 or 5.
redirect_script.praise: You estimated each number, then checked both ends of the range.

vocabulary.definition: A number that can be written as a fraction of integers, including whole numbers and terminating decimals.
A number whose decimal never ends or repeats, like the square root of a non-perfect square.

worked_example_script.text: Write the range 'greater than 2 and less than 6' and the list: the square root of 8, 5.5, the square root of 40, 1.
Estimate each. Which are greater than 2 AND less than 6?
The square root of 8 is about 2.8 (in), 5.5 is in, the square root of 40 is about 6.3 (out, too big), 1 is out. So the square root of 8 and 5.5.
If a student leaves out the square root of 8, ask 'about how big is the square root of 8 -- did you estimate it?'
Your turn: from the square root of 5, 4.5, the square root of 50, pick those greater than 2 and less than 5.

practice_problems.answer: Yes

practice_problems.stem: Is 6 greater than 1.5 and less than 5?
practice_problems.answer: No, 6 is too big

practice_problems.stem: Select all greater than 1.5 and less than 5: the square root of 3, the square root of 10, 4.5, 6, the square root of 30.
practice_problems.answer: the square root of 3, the square root of 10, 4.5

practice_problems.stem: Select all greater than 2 and less than 4: the square root of 5, the square root of 13, 3.5, the square root of 20, 1.5.
practice_problems.answer: the square root of 5, the square root of 13, 3.5

practice_problems.stem: For 'greater than 1.5 and less than 5,' Sam sorted the square roots. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Sam kept only 4.5, saying 'the square root of 10 is 10, too big, and the square root of 3 is 3, too big -- both out.'
practice_problems.answer: Sam used the number under the root instead of estimating. The square root of 10 is about 3.2 and the square root of 3 is about 1.7 -- both are in the range. Only 6 and the square root of 30 (about 5.5) are out.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: comparing to the radicand.

practice_problems.stem: Select all greater than 4.5 and less than 8: the square root of 30, 7, the square root of 17, the square root of 50, 9.
practice_problems.answer: the square root of 30, 7, the square root of 50

practice_problems.stem: Write one irrational number and one rational number that both fall between 3 and 4.
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 13 (about 3.6) and 3.5 (or any decimal in that interval).

practice_problems.stem: Explain why the square root of 30 is NOT between 1.5 and 5, using an estimate.
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 30 is about 5.5 (between 5 and 6), which is greater than 5, so it falls outside the range.

activities.title: In the Range or Out
activities.instructions:
1. Post the range 'greater than 2 and less than 6.'
2. Sort each number card into 'In the range' or 'Out.'
3. For each card, estimate its value and check both ends.
4. Debrief: which cards were close to a boundary, and how did you decide?

activities.title: Estimate, Then Compare
activities.instructions:
1. Read that Sam excluded the square root of 10 and the square root of 3 from 'greater than 1.5 and less than 5.'
2. Estimate each square root to a decimal.
3. Decide which numbers really belong in the range.
4. Write the one step Sam skipped.

content.worked_problem: For 'greater than 1.5 and less than 5,' Sam excluded the square root of 10 and the square root of 3.
content.error_step: Sam judged the roots by the number under them (10 and 3) instead of estimating.
content.why: The square root of 10 is about 3.2 and the square root of 3 is about 1.7 -- both are in the range.

activities.title: Range Roundup
materials: Tape to mark a zone on the floor
activities.instructions:
1. Tape a zone on the floor and label it with a range.
2. Hand out number cards (mix of roots and rationals).
3. On a signal, each student estimates and steps into the zone only if their number fits.
4. Debrief: which roots were borderline, and how did estimating settle it?

strategy_links.why: Comparing a root to its radicand is a precise error a find-and-fix targets.
Debating 'is the square root of 30 in or out' surfaces the estimate-first reasoning.
Sharing quick estimates for each number builds fluent comparison against both bounds.

questioning_prompts: What is each square root worth as a decimal?
Is the value greater than the low end AND less than the high end?
Did you compare using the estimate, or the number under the root?
Which numbers are borderline, and how did you decide?
How can you check a value that is close to a boundary?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares an irrational number to the range using the radicand or half of it instead of its estimate.
misconception_redirects.say: Turn every square root into a decimal first: the square root of 10 is about 3.2, so it is greater than 1.5 and less than 5 -- it belongs in the range. Don't compare using 10 or 5.
misconception_redirects.praise: You estimated each number, then checked both ends of the range.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student checks only one bound and forgets the other.
misconception_redirects.say: A number must pass BOTH tests: greater than the low end and less than the high end. The square root of 40 is about 6.3 -- greater than 2, but not less than 6, so it's out.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked both ends before keeping the number.

quick_checks.prompt: Is the square root of 10 greater than 1.5 and less than 5?
quick_checks.look_for: Yes (about 3.2). A 'no' means the student used 10 instead of estimating.

quick_checks.prompt: Is the square root of 30 between 1.5 and 5?
quick_checks.look_for: No (about 5.5, too big). 'Yes' may mean halving to 3 or skipping the upper bound.

sentence_starters: The square root of ___ is about ___, which is ___ the range.
I checked both ends: greater than ___ and less than ___.

steps.math: the square root of 8 is about 2.8

steps.math: 2.8 is greater than 2 and less than 6 -- IN
5.5 is IN; the square root of 40 is about 6.3 -- OUT (too big); 1 is OUT (too small)

skills.name: Compare an irrational number to a rational number using approximation
skills.i_do_script: To compare an irrational number to a rational one, I estimate the irrational number, then compare the two values. Watch: is the square root of 30 greater than 5? The square root of 30 is about 5.5, and 5.5 > 5, so the statement is true. Is the square root of 30 greater than 6? 5.5 is not greater than 6, so that one is false. I estimate first, then read the inequality -- I never divide 30 by 2, which would wrongly suggest 15.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares the rational number to the radicand or half of it instead of the estimated root
canonical_error.example: Marks 'the square root of 30 > 6' as true because 30 is greater than 6, instead of estimating the root as about 5.5
canonical_error.why: The student compares using the number under the root rather than its value. The square root of 30 is about 5.5, so it is greater than 5 but not greater than 6.

skills.item_template: True/False comparisons between a square root and a rational number. True/false.

sample_items.stem: True or False: the square root of 30 > 5.
True or False: the square root of 30 > 6.
True or False: the square root of 13 < 4.
True or False: the square root of 50 < 7.

redirect_script.stop: Estimate the root before you compare.
redirect_script.prompt: Replace the square root with its estimate: the square root of 30 is about 5.5. Now compare 5.5 to the number. 5.5 > 5 is true; 5.5 > 6 is false. Don't compare using 30.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the estimate to the number -- that's how to judge the inequality.

vocabulary.definition: A statement that one value is greater than or less than another, using > or <.
A value close enough to compare with, found from nearby perfect squares.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'the square root of 40 > 6' and 'the square root of 40 < 6.'
About how big is the square root of 40? Which statement is true?
The square root of 40 is about 6.3, so the square root of 40 > 6 is true and the square root of 40 < 6 is false.
If a student marks the square root of 40 > 6 false, ask 'what did you estimate the square root of 40 to be?'
Your turn: true or false -- the square root of 20 < 4?

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 30 is about 5.5. Is it greater than 5?
practice_problems.answer: Yes

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 13 is about 3.6. Is it less than 4?
practice_problems.answer: Yes

practice_problems.stem: True or False: the square root of 30 > 6.
practice_problems.answer: False (about 5.5)

practice_problems.stem: True or False: the square root of 50 > 7.
practice_problems.answer: True (about 7.07)

practice_problems.stem: Alex compared the square root of 30 to 6. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Alex wrote: 'the square root of 30 > 6 is TRUE, because 30 is bigger than 6.'
practice_problems.answer: Alex compared 30 to 6 instead of estimating the root. The square root of 30 is about 5.5, which is NOT greater than 6, so the statement is false.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: comparing the radicand, not the root.

practice_problems.stem: Order from least to greatest: the square root of 20, 4, the square root of 13.
practice_problems.answer: the square root of 13 (about 3.6), 4, the square root of 20 (about 4.5)

practice_problems.stem: Write a true inequality comparing the square root of 55 to a whole number.

practice_problems.answer: 25 < 30 < 36 puts it between 5 and 6; the square root of 30 is about 5.48, which is just less than 5.5.
practice_problems.notes: Reason and compare to a decimal.

activities.title: True or False
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the comparison cards.
2. Sort each into 'True' or 'False.'
3. For each card, estimate the square root and compare it to the rational number.
4. Debrief: which false cards came from comparing the number under the root?

activities.title: Compare the Root, Not the Number
activities.instructions:

2. Estimate the square root of 30 using the perfect squares around it.

content.error_step: Alex compared 30 to 6 instead of the estimated root 5.5.
content.why: The square root of 30 is about 5.5, which is not greater than 6, so the statement is false.

activities.title: Root to a True Comparison
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the square-root cards and the comparison cards.
2. Match each root to the true 'is between' statement.
3. Justify with the perfect squares that bracket the number.
4. Debrief: which decoy came from halving?

strategy_links.why: Comparing the radicand instead of the root is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects.
Defending true/false calls surfaces the estimate-then-compare reasoning.
Modeling 'I estimate the root, then read the inequality' makes the comparison routine visible.

Are you comparing the estimate, or the number under the root?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares the rational number to the radicand or half of it instead of the estimated root.
misconception_redirects.say: Replace the square root with its estimate: the square root of 30 is about 5.5. Now compare 5.5 to the number. 5.5 > 5 is true; 5.5 > 6 is false. Don't compare using 30.

misconception_redirects.praise: You read the inequality in the right direction after estimating.

True or False: the square root of 50 > 7.
quick_checks.look_for: True (about 7.07). 'False' means the estimate was too low.

skills.name: Estimate and compare values of expressions involving irrational numbers
skills.i_do_script: To compare expressions that include an irrational number, I estimate the irrational part, do the one operation, then compare. Watch: is the square root of 2 + 3 greater than 4? The square root of 2 is about 1.4, so the square root of 2 + 3 is about 4.4, which is greater than 4 -- true. For 3 times pi, I use pi is about 3.14, so 3 times pi is about 9.4. I estimate the irrational piece to a decimal, then finish the arithmetic; I never treat the square root of 2 as 1 (rounding too hard) or halving it.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops or over-rounds the irrational part before doing the operation
canonical_error.example: Estimates the square root of 2 + 3 as 4 by calling the square root of 2 equal to 1, instead of about 1.4 for a value near 4.4
canonical_error.why: The student replaces the irrational number with a whole number that is too rough (or halves it), so the expression's estimate is off by enough to flip a comparison.

skills.item_template: Expressions combining an irrational number and one operation, compared to a benchmark. Multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Select all expressions greater than 4: the square root of 2 + 3, pi + 2, the square root of 10 - 1, 2.
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(2)+3 ~ 4.4 and pi+2 ~ 5.14 exceed 4; sqrt(10)-1 ~ 2.16 and 2 do not.

sample_items.stem: Select all expressions greater than 5: 3 times pi, the square root of 2 + 3, pi + 2, the square root of 5 + 1.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3pi ~ 9.42 and pi+2 ~ 5.14 exceed 5; sqrt(2)+3 ~ 4.41 and sqrt(5)+1 ~ 3.24 do not.

sample_items.stem: Select all expressions greater than 2 and 3/4: the square root of 5 + 1, 0.4 + 3, 4 - 0.3, the square root of 2.
Select all expressions greater than 6: 3 times pi, the square root of 50, pi - 1, the square root of 40.
sample_items.answer: 3 times pi, the square root of 50, the square root of 40
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3pi ~ 9.42, sqrt(50) ~ 7.07, sqrt(40) ~ 6.32 exceed 6; pi-1 ~ 2.14 does not.

redirect_script.prompt: Replace the irrational piece with a decimal, then do the one operation: the square root of 2 is about 1.4, so the square root of 2 + 3 is about 4.4. Now compare 4.4 to the benchmark. Don't treat the square root of 2 as 1.
redirect_script.praise: You estimated the irrational part, finished the operation, then compared.

vocabulary.definition: A math phrase combining numbers and one operation, such as the square root of 2 + 3.
A number whose decimal never ends or repeats, like the square root of a non-perfect square or a multiple of pi.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for AI.NF.1 (the real number system and radicals in Algebra I).

practice_problems.stem: Riley compared the square root of 2 + 3 to 4. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Riley wrote: 'the square root of 2 + 3 = 4, because the square root of 2 is about 1, so 1 + 3 = 4 -- not greater than 4.'
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 2 is about 1.4, not 1, so the square root of 2 + 3 is about 4.4 -- which IS greater than 4. Rounding the root down to 1 lost the comparison.

practice_problems.stem: Is 3 times pi greater than 9?
practice_problems.answer: Yes (about 9.4)

practice_problems.answer: For example, the square root of 10 + 2 (about 5.2), or 3 + the square root of 8 (about 5.8).

practice_problems.answer: Pi + 2 is about 5.14 and the square root of 2 + 3 is about 4.41, so pi + 2 is larger by about 0.7.

activities.title: Greater Than 5 or Not
activities.instructions:

2. Sort each into 'Greater than 5' or 'Not greater than 5.'
3. For each card, estimate the irrational part, do the operation, then compare.

activities.title: Don't Round the Root to a Whole Number
activities.instructions:
1. Read Riley's claim that the square root of 2 + 3 = 4, using the square root of 2 = 1.
2. Estimate the square root of 2 to a tenth.
3. Redo the expression and compare to 4.
4. Write why rounding the root to 1 changed the answer.

content.worked_problem: Is the square root of 2 + 3 greater than 4? Riley used the square root of 2 = 1 to get 4.
content.error_step: Riley rounded the square root of 2 down to 1 instead of about 1.4.
content.why: The square root of 2 is about 1.4, so the expression is about 4.4 -- greater than 4.

activities.title: Beat the Benchmark
activities.instructions:
1. Draw an expression card and a benchmark card.
2. Each player estimates the irrational part and does the one operation.
3. Declare 'greater' or 'less' and defend it with your decimal estimate.
4. Debrief: which expressions were too close to call quickly, and why?

strategy_links.why: Studying a correct estimate beside an over-rounded one targets the drop-the-root error.
Debating which expressions beat the benchmark builds estimate-then-operate reasoning.
Writing out 'estimate the irrational part, then do the operation' consolidates the multi-step routine.

misconception_redirects.praise: You estimated the irrational part, finished the operation, then compared.

quick_checks.look_for: Yes (about 4.4). A 'no' means the student used sqrt(2) = 1.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (identify which two whole numbers a square root lies between) -- the bracketing move the whole standard rests on. If they pass, move up: S5 (compare an irrational number to a rational one) and S6 (estimate and compare expressions). If they fail, split: S1 checks whether they can even round a root to the nearest whole number, and S2 checks plotting on a number line. S4 (select all numbers in a range) branches off as the multi-number application of the bracket.
